canonicalExplanation.summary: Valid, semantic markup is only half the job — the **words** must be clear too. A semantic content review checks each page with a **traceable checklist**: do headings describe their sections? Is link text unique and specific? Are acronyms explained on first use? Are instructions short and plain? Do alt texts and error messages actually help? Each finding is written down with its location and fix, so nothing is fixed by memory.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
The course page validates and uses perfect landmarks. Yet learners write in: "Which 'Learn more' is the HTML course?" and "What does LMS mean?" The structure is right; the words aren't. A reviewer replaces three Learn more links with destination-specific names and simplifies an unexplained acronym. In this lesson you'll produce a traceable review checklist and repair semantic inconsistencies.

```predict
{"question": "The page uses `<h2>` correctly for every section. Does that make the headings clear?", "options": ["Yes, semantic elements guarantee clarity", "No — \"Section 2\" is valid but tells readers nothing"], "answer": 1, "why": "Elements give structure; only the words inside give meaning. Review both."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Metadata and accessibility audit**, **Images and media**, **Data tables** and **Forms and native controls** modules, plus **Markup conformance** and the **Keyboard and accessibility-tree audit**.

sections.heading: The model: a checklist that leaves a trail
sections.body:
| Check | Pass when |
|---|---|
| page title and h1. | unique, and they match the page's purpose. |
| headings. | each names what its section contains. |
| link text. | unique and describes the destination. |
| acronyms and jargon. | explained on first use, or replaced with plain words. |
| alt text. | fits the image's job. |
| form labels and errors. | say what to enter and how to fix it. |

**Record format:** page · element · check failed · original text · new text · reviewer · date.

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why write findings down instead of just fixing them?", "answer": "A trail lets others verify the fix, spot patterns across pages (\"we use 'Learn more' everywhere\"), and recheck later."}
```

sections.heading: Consistency across pages

includes: Review headings, links, acronyms, alt text and form text with a checklist.
Record findings traceably and fix inconsistent wording across pages.

outcomes: Produce a traceable review checklist and repair semantic inconsistencies.

examples.title: Fixing three "Learn more" links
examples.situation: A reviewer replaces three Learn more links with destination-specific names and simplifies an unexplained acronym.
walkthrough: **Check link text:** three cards say "Learn more"; the checklist fails "unique and describes the destination".
**Replace:** "Learn more about HTML", "…CSS", "…JavaScript" — destination-specific names recorded with the old text.
**Acronym:** "Access it via the LMS" becomes "Access it in your course dashboard"; the reviewer will read the page aloud to validate it.
examples.result: The links read clearly out of context, the acronym is gone, and every change is logged.

examples.title: The mismatched title
examples.situation: A page titled "Pricing – Codestead" has the h1 "Plans" and a nav link "Costs".
walkthrough: Three names for one page confuse users and search results.
The checklist fails "title and h1 match the page's purpose".
Fix: use "Pricing" in the title, h1 and nav link; record it.
examples.result: One consistent name identifies the page everywhere.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Semantic elements automatically make the words inside them clear and accessible.
misconceptions.correction: Elements provide structure and roles, but clarity comes from the text: specific headings, unique link names, explained acronyms and helpful messages. Review the content itself with a checklist.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Fixing three Learn more links", which checklist item failed?

analogy.example: A content review is like **proof-reading a building's signage**: the signs are in the right places (semantics), but "Room" on every door still gets people lost. Each fix goes in the maintenance log.
limitations: Signs are physical; web text can be updated instantly.
Consistency matters in both — one name per place.

farTransfer.prompt: Create a review checklist for your own site and run it on three pages. Log every finding, fix them, and note any pattern that repeats across pages.
expectedEvidence: Completed checklist with logged findings for three pages.

remediation.explanation: Read only the headings, then only the links, then only the buttons and errors — each list must make sense on its own. Log every item that doesn't.

recap.summary: To produce a traceable review checklist and repair semantic inconsistencies, check titles, headings, link text, acronyms, alt text and form wording page by page, record each finding with its location and fix, and use one consistent term for each thing across the site.
